name: Nuwakot
tagline: The hill fort where Prithvi Narayan Shah planned Nepal
meta_description: Nuwakot: the seven-storey palace of Prithvi Narayan Shah, Bhairavi temple and Sindure Jatra, 75 km from Kathmandu. History, how to reach, where to stay.
summary: Nuwakot is a ridge-top fort town about 75 km north-west of Kathmandu, above the Trishuli and Tadi rivers. Its seven-storey palace was built by Prithvi Narayan Shah after he took the fort in 1744, and from here he planned the conquest of the Kathmandu Valley. Stay one night.
intro: Nuwakot sits on a ridge at about 900 m, where the Tadi river meets the Trishuli. For more than a thousand years the hill served as a lookout guarding the western approach to the Kathmandu Valley and the trade road to Tibet through Kerung. The word kot means fort, and the old name Nawakot is often explained as nine forts: the hill was one of a ring of strongholds watching the valley below. Today it is a quiet farming village with a brick palace tower rising above its tiled roofs.

Most travellers come for Nuwakot Durbar, the seven-storey palace locals call Sat Talle Durbar, and for the temple of Bhairavi just south of it. The complex was badly damaged by the April 2015 earthquake and has been under restoration since. Walking around it you see Newar craftsmanship: carved windows, glazed tile roofs, brick laid in the Kathmandu style, because craftsmen from Lalitpur built it. The site has been on UNESCO's tentative list since 2008.

Nuwakot is also a place to slow down. Mornings bring mist in the Trishuli valley, children walking to school along the ridge and farmers cutting fodder on the terraces. A night here pairs well with a Langtang trek or a drive toward Gorkha. The valley floor below, at Bidur and Trishuli Bazaar, was hit hard by the flood of 26 August 2026; the ridge-top town was spared, but check current status before you travel.

story.title: The fort that opened the road to Kathmandu
paras: In the 1740s Nuwakot belonged to Kantipur, the Malla kingdom of Kathmandu, and it mattered: whoever held the hill controlled the trade route from the valley to Tibet. Gorkha, a small hill kingdom to the west, had already failed once to take it. When the young Prithvi Narayan Shah became king of Gorkha he prepared carefully, bought arms and trained his troops, and on 26 September 1744, a day his astrologer had chosen, attacked the fort. Within days Nuwakot was his. Jaya Prakash Malla of Kantipur tried to win it back the next year and failed.

Prithvi Narayan Shah moved his base to Nuwakot and used it as the staging ground for the long campaign that ended with the fall of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur in 1768 and 1769. On the ridge he built the seven-storey palace as both residence and fortress, with walls about 6 feet thick. The ground floor held guards and courtiers, the king and queen lived higher up, and the fifth and sixth floors were used as a prison: the king of Tanahun was held here. Prithvi Narayan Shah died in Nuwakot in 1775.

Nuwakot stayed important after him. In 1792, during the war with China, Qing troops came close to the fort. In 1793 the British envoy William Kirkpatrick met the regent Bahadur Shah here, and that same year Bahadur Shah fixed a copper plate at the Bhairavi temple recording Nepal's victory and stored captured weapons inside it. Then the capital's business moved to Kathmandu and Nuwakot became a farming village again. The 2015 earthquake cracked the palace and toppled temples; restoration has been slow and careful, and the Bhairavi temple was reopened in 2020.

legend: Temple tradition at Nuwakot says the goddess Bhairavi protects the fort and its people, and her chief priest, the dhami, is bound to her territory. By old custom the dhami may not cross the Trishuli or the Tadi rivers without the king's permission, and when he dies the office passes to his eldest son. During Sindure Jatra the dhami is believed to carry the goddess, and people bring him their troubles and questions.
people: Nuwakot's old bazaar is a Newar town: families who came with the palace builders and traders and still keep the guthi trusts that fund temple rituals. Around them on the slopes live Brahmin and Chhetri farmers, and further up the hills Tamang villages. People grow rice in the valley, maize and millet on the terraces, and oranges and vegetables for Kathmandu. Many young people work in Kathmandu or abroad and come home for festivals.

untold.fact: The fifth and sixth floors of Nuwakot's seven-storey palace were used as a prison. Among those held there were the king of Tanahun, Tri Bikram Sen, and Bal Narsingh of Kirtipur.

In 1793 Bahadur Shah installed a copper plate at Nuwakot's Bhairavi temple declaring Nepal's victory in the war with China, stored seized weapons on the temple's second storey, and gave it the copper roof it still has.

Nuwakot was the meeting place, in 1793, of the British envoy Captain William Kirkpatrick and the acting regent Bahadur Shah, one of the first formal contacts between Nepal and the British East India Company.

local_words.meaning: Fort; the root of the town's name
A community trust that funds and runs temple rituals and festivals

taste.name: Trishuli river fish and sel roti
taste.text: Along the Trishuli, small roadside kitchens fry river fish in mustard oil with chilli and turmeric, eaten with beaten rice. Up on the ridge, homes make sel roti, a crisp ring of sweet rice batter, at festivals. Ask at The Famous Farm or a bazaar tea shop for a home-cooked dal bhat with local greens.

facts: Seven-storey palace, Bhairavi temple, Sindure Jatra

highlights.title: Sat Talle Durbar
highlights.text: The seven-storey brick palace of Prithvi Narayan Shah, built like a fort with walls about 6 feet thick and carved Newar windows. Damaged in 2015 and under restoration, it is still the most dramatic building between Kathmandu and the Tibetan border.

highlights.title: Bhairavi temple
highlights.text: A pagoda temple about 200 m south of the palace, dedicated to the protector goddess of Nuwakot. Look for the stone and metal lions at the door, the figures holding sindur beside the stairs, and the copper roof fixed in 1793.

highlights.title: Taleju hill
highlights.text: A short climb from the palace leads to the five-tiered Taleju Bhawani temple, the Malla family goddess, believed to date from around the 1400s. The view takes in the Trishuli and Tadi valleys and, on clear days, Ganesh Himal.

highlights.title: Sindure Jatra
highlights.text: Nuwakot's spring festival, when the yosin pole goes up, the dhami lead processions between the goddess temples and the whole crowd ends up red with sindur powder. It runs through April and into early May.

highlights.title: Ridge walks and village lanes
highlights.text: Paths run along the ridge through terraced fields, small Newar and Brahmin hamlets and orange orchards. A two-hour loop at sunrise or late afternoon shows how the fort town looks over both river valleys.

how_to_reach.text: About 75 km from Kathmandu via Balaju, Kakani and Bidur (Trishuli Bazaar), then 7 km up to the ridge: 3 to 3.5 hours by private car. Buses run from Machhapokhari to Bidur. The valley floor was hit by the flood of 26 August 2026; check current status before you travel.
From Bidur an old trail climbs through farmland to the palace in 1.5 to 2 hours. It is pleasant in the cool months and avoids the road.

where_to_stay: Stay on the ridge rather than in Bidur. The Famous Farm, a restored Newar farmhouse in the old bazaar a few minutes from the palace, is our first choice: simple rooms, courtyard meals and a view down the Trishuli valley. A few small guesthouses and homestays in the village offer basic rooms with shared bathrooms. Bidur has local hotels near the bus park, useful only if you arrive late, and parts of Trishuli Bazaar were damaged by the August 2026 flood.
tips: Visit the palace in late afternoon when the light warms the brick and the tour groups have gone.
Carry small notes for the palace entry ticket and temple offerings; there is no reliable ATM on the ridge.
Dress modestly near the Bhairavi temple and take off leather before entering temple courtyards where asked.
In April and May the valley floor is hot, above 30 °C; walk early and rest at midday.
Check road conditions through Bidur before setting out, as flood repairs may cause delays.

experiences.title: Seven-storey palace history walk
experiences.summary: Walk the palace complex with a guide who tells the story of the 1744 siege, the Gorkha campaign and the king's last years here, from the guard house to the Ranga Mahal theatre and the house of Rana Bahadur Shah.
body: We start outside the walls, where you can see how the palace was sited: on the highest point of the ridge with drops on two sides and a clear view up the Trishuli toward Tibet. The main tower is 84 by 36 feet at its base, with a main door facing east. Your guide explains how the floors were used, from the guard rooms at the bottom to the king's rooms, a prayer room higher up, and the floors used as a prison.

Around the main palace stand the smaller buildings: the Garad Ghar where soldiers and ammunition were kept, the Ranga Mahal where kings watched dance and theatre, and the house built for King Rana Bahadur Shah in 1795, ruined by 1957 and rebuilt later. Some areas may be closed for restoration work after the 2015 earthquake, so the route changes a little from year to year.

The walk ends at the edge of the ridge as the light goes, looking down on the Trishuli. Here we tell the later story: the Chinese army close to Nuwakot in 1792, the British envoy in 1793, and the slow return to village life once Kathmandu became the capital. It is a good hour for photographs of the tower against the hills.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Nuwakot palace?
faqs.a: Yes, the Nuwakot Durbar complex charges an entry ticket, with a higher rate for foreign visitors than for Nepali and SAARC citizens. Prices are set by the authorities and change, so check current status before you travel. Keep small notes ready, since card payment is not reliable on the ridge. Your guide's fee is separate.

faqs.q: Can you go inside the seven-storey tower?
faqs.a: Access depends on the state of restoration work after the 2015 earthquake. In some years visitors could enter lower floors; at other times the tower was closed while engineers strengthened it. We check before each visit. Even when the interior is shut, the courtyards, outer buildings and temples around it make the walk worthwhile.

faqs.q: How long should I spend at Nuwakot palace?
faqs.a: Two to three hours covers the palace complex, the Bhairavi temple and the climb to the Taleju temple at an easy pace with time for photographs. Add an hour if you want to walk through the village lanes and sit at a tea shop. Staying overnight lets you see the site at both sunset and sunrise.

experiences.title: Bhairavi and Taleju temple circuit
experiences.summary: A morning loop to the temples that guard the fort: the Bhairavi pagoda where offerings start at dawn, the old Narayan temple near the guard house, and the hill-top Taleju Bhawani temple of the Malla kings.
body: Nuwakot's temples are older than the Shah palace. The Narayan and Vishnu temples near the guard house date to the Malla period, and an inscription of Ripu Malla from 1498 was found here. The five-tiered Taleju Bhawani temple, on a small hill about 150 m from the palace, honours the family goddess of the Malla kings and is thought to date from around the 1400s. Worship there still continues at festivals.

The Bhairavi temple, 200 m south of the palace, is the living heart of Nuwakot. At dawn people come with rice, flowers and vermilion, ring the bells and walk around the shrine clockwise. The temple faces west, and figures holding sindur stand on either side of the main stairs. It was badly damaged in 2015 and restored by August 2020.

We walk the loop slowly with a local guide who can explain the rituals and who the dhami is. There is also a stupa on the north side of the palace, restored by Prithvi Narayan Shah according to its inscription, which reminds you that Buddhist and Hindu worship have always lived side by side on this ridge.

faqs.q: Can non-Hindus enter the Bhairavi temple in Nuwakot?
faqs.a: Visitors can walk around the temple courtyard and watch worship, but the inner sanctum is for worshippers and priests. Follow your guide, do not touch offerings or images, remove shoes where asked and avoid leather near the shrine. Photography of the exterior is generally fine; ask before photographing people at prayer.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit the Nuwakot temples?
faqs.a: Early morning, from about 6 to 8 am, is when local people come to worship and the light is soft. Tuesdays and Saturdays are busier days for goddess temples in Nepal. In spring, during Sindure Jatra, the temples are the centre of processions and much more crowded, which is worth planning for.

faqs.q: How difficult is the walk to the Taleju temple?
faqs.a: It is a short climb of about 10 minutes on stone steps from the palace area, fine for most people who can manage stairs. There are no handrails on some sections and steps can be uneven, so take care after rain. The view from the top over the Trishuli and Tadi valleys is worth the effort.

experiences.title: Sunrise ridge walk through farm villages
experiences.summary: An easy walk along the Nuwakot ridge at first light, through terraced fields, orange orchards and small hamlets, with mist lying in the Trishuli valley below and Ganesh Himal visible on clear winter mornings.
body: We leave the bazaar before sunrise and follow farm paths along the ridge. On clear days from October to February the snow peaks of Ganesh Himal and the Langtang range appear to the north as the sun comes up, while the river valleys below stay in mist. It is the hour when village life starts: smoke from kitchen fires, buffaloes being taken to water, children in school uniforms walking the ridge.

The path passes terraces of rice, maize and millet depending on the season, and orange trees heavy with fruit in November and December. Your guide stops to talk with farmers, explains what grows when, and points out the lines of the old fort network on the surrounding hills that gave Nuwakot its strategic value.

We loop back to the bazaar for breakfast. The walk is mostly level with a few short climbs, about 6 to 8 km depending on the route chosen. It is a simple, quiet way to understand why kings fought over this ridge, and why people still choose to farm here.

faqs.q: Can you see the Himalaya from Nuwakot?
faqs.a: On clear days, mostly from October to February, you can see Ganesh Himal and parts of the Langtang range to the north, best at sunrise before haze builds. In spring the view is often hazy by mid-morning, and from June to September cloud usually hides the mountains. Nuwakot is a heritage stop first; mountain views are a bonus.

faqs.q: Is the Nuwakot ridge walk suitable for children?
faqs.a: Yes. It is on village paths with gentle ups and downs, about 6 to 8 km, and can be shortened. Children usually enjoy the animals, orchards and village life. Bring water, snacks and warm layers for the early start, since winter mornings are around 5 to 8 °C on the ridge before the sun reaches it.

faqs.q: When is orange season in Nuwakot?
faqs.a: Oranges ripen from about November to January in the hills around Nuwakot, and you will see fruit on the trees and for sale at the roadside. It is a good season to visit in general: dry, clear mornings and comfortable daytime temperatures of around 18 to 22 °C.

experiences.title: Farm kitchen dal bhat at Nuwakot
experiences.summary: Help pick greens in a farm garden and cook a Nepali dinner over a wood or gas fire: lentils, rice, seasonal vegetables, pickle and, at festival times, sel roti. Then eat it in the courtyard as the bells ring at the Bhairavi temple.
body: Dal bhat is the daily meal of Nepal, and in a farm kitchen in Nuwakot it changes with the season. In winter it might be mustard greens, radish and cauliflower; in spring, young pumpkin shoots and fresh coriander; in autumn, after the rice harvest, the new rice itself. We arrange the session at The Famous Farm or with a family in the village, depending on the season.

You start in the garden, picking what is ready, then learn the basic steps: tempering lentils with ghee, cumin and garlic, frying greens with fenugreek seed, and pounding a fresh tomato and sesame achar. Your cook explains the small rules of a Nepali kitchen, such as keeping the hearth clean and eating with the right hand.

Dinner is served on brass or steel plates in the courtyard. If it is a festival season you may also see sel roti being fried, rings of sweet rice batter. The session is relaxed and hands-on, and you leave with the method to repeat at home.

faqs.q: Is the Nuwakot cooking session vegetarian?
faqs.a: The core dal bhat is vegetarian, and we can keep the whole meal vegetarian or vegan if you ask in advance; ghee can be replaced with oil. Families in Nuwakot also cook chicken or goat curry for guests on request. Tell us about allergies, especially to nuts, sesame or mustard, which are common in Nepali cooking.

faqs.q: Do I need cooking experience for the farm kitchen class?
faqs.a: No. The class is hands-on but simple, and the cook guides each step. Children can help with picking vegetables and rolling or shaping dough. Expect a home kitchen, not a cooking school: low stools, a wood or gas stove and a small working space, which is part of the charm.

faqs.q: How long does the cooking session last?
faqs.a: About two hours including garden picking, cooking and eating. It is usually held in the late afternoon so dinner is ready around dusk. If you are staying at The Famous Farm, it can replace your included dinner. Timing is flexible, and we can shift it to lunch on a day trip.

faqs.q: Why is Nuwakot important in Nepal's history?
faqs.a: Nuwakot was the fort that guarded the western approach to the Kathmandu Valley and the trade route to Tibet. Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha captured it in 1744 and used it as his base for the campaign that ended with the conquest of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur in 1768 and 1769. He built the seven-storey palace here and died in Nuwakot in 1775.

faqs.q: How do I get from Kathmandu to Nuwakot?
faqs.a: By road, about 75 km via Kakani and Bidur (Trishuli Bazaar), then up to the ridge. A private car takes 3 to 3.5 hours; buses to Bidur take longer, and local jeeps or taxis cover the last 7 km. After the 26 August 2026 flood in the Trishuli valley there may be detours; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Was Nuwakot affected by the 2026 Trishuli flood?
faqs.a: The palace and old bazaar on the ridge were not in the flood's path. The valley floor below was: Trishuli Bazaar in Bidur lost a bridge, buildings and water supplies, and Devighat downstream was flooded. Bidur served as a base for rescue operations. Road access may still involve detours, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Nuwakot palace open after the earthquake?
faqs.a: The complex was badly damaged in April 2015 and has been under long restoration. The grounds, courtyards and surrounding temples have been open to visitors, with some buildings closed during work. The Bhairavi temple was restored by August 2020. Access to the interior of the tower varies, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in Nuwakot?
faqs.a: One night is enough to see the palace, temples and village and to walk the ridge at sunrise. Two nights let you slow down, join a cooking session and walk further into the farm hills. Many of our travellers add Nuwakot at the start or end of a Langtang trek, or between Kathmandu and Gorkha.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Nuwakot?
faqs.a: October to April. Autumn and winter mornings are clear, with Himalayan views from the ridge, and days are around 18 to 24 °C. March and April are warmer and bring Sindure Jatra. May is hot in the valley, above 30 °C, and June to September is monsoon, with heavy rain, leeches and slow roads.

faqs.q: What is Sindure Jatra in Nuwakot?
faqs.a: It is the spring festival of the goddess Bhairavi, held across Chaitra and Baisakh (roughly April to early May). A wooden yosin pole is raised at the goddess temples, the dhami and guthi members lead processions to the Taleju temple, and people smear each other with red sindur. Dates move each year; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where should I stay in Nuwakot?
faqs.a: On the ridge, near the palace. The Famous Farm, a restored Newar farmhouse with courtyard meals, is the most comfortable option and a few minutes' walk from the Durbar. Small village guesthouses and homestays offer simpler rooms. Avoid staying in Bidur unless you arrive late, as the valley floor is hot and was damaged in the August 2026 flood.

faqs.q: Can I combine Nuwakot with a Langtang trek?
faqs.a: Yes. Nuwakot lies near the road from Kathmandu to Dhunche and Syabrubesi, so one night here before the trek breaks the long drive and adds history. Coming back, it is a calm place to rest after the mountains. Since the August 2026 flood the Syabrubesi road has been disrupted; check current status before you travel.
